questions.q: DispatchDB is in the FULL recovery model but has never had a transaction log backup. What is the concrete symptom of this on MERSQL01?
options: The transaction log file has grown to 210 GB because nothing is ever clearing it, filling up the C: drive
The database silently switches itself to SIMPLE recovery
Full backups become impossible until a log backup runs
There is no symptom — FULL recovery with no log backups is a supported, low-risk configuration
questions.explain: In FULL recovery, the log can't reuse space until a log backup (or equivalent) checkpoints it out. With no log backups ever taken, the log keeps growing indefinitely, which is exactly what happened to DispatchDB_log.ldf.

questions.q: Why is DispatchTrack's app connecting to MERSQL01 as the sa login a serious security problem, beyond just the weak password?
options: sa is a sysadmin-level account, so any compromise of the app's connection string grants full control of the entire instance, not just DispatchDB
sa cannot run T-SQL, so the app would only be able to use it for authentication
It isn't actually a problem as long as mixed mode authentication is enabled
sa only has read access by default, so the risk is limited
questions.explain: sa is a member of the sysadmin fixed server role by default. An app connecting as sa means anyone who reads that connection string — or exploits an injection flaw in the app — gets full administrative control of MERSQL01, not just DispatchDB.

questions.q: What does msdb.dbo.sysjobs having only one disabled row tell a new DBA doing discovery on MERSQL01?
options: There is effectively no automated maintenance running — no backups, index maintenance, or integrity checks are scheduled
SQL Server Agent is not installed on this instance
The server has too many jobs and needs cleanup
msdb is corrupted and needs to be rebuilt
questions.explain: sysjobs holds one row per Agent job. A single disabled leftover row means nothing meaningful is scheduled — no backup jobs, no index maintenance, no integrity checks — which matches the rest of the discovery findings.

questions.q: Why does this capstone tackle the server in a specific order — architecture/storage first, then security, then maintenance automation, then incident and change management — rather than jumping straight to the sa login problem?
options: Because a stable, correctly configured foundation (storage, tempdb, memory) has to be in place before security hardening and automated maintenance can be trusted to run reliably
Order doesn't matter; it's presented this way only for narrative convenience
Security must always be fixed before anything else, and this order violates that rule
Because SQL Server enforces this order technically and won't allow jobs to be created before sa is disabled
questions.explain: The plan mirrors the course's own structure: you can't reliably automate maintenance or lock down access on storage/configuration that's still broken (log filling the disk, misconfigured tempdb), so stabilization comes first.

questions.q: What is an RPO (Recovery Point Objective), and why is it effectively 'undefined' for DispatchDB as inherited?
options: It's how much data loss is acceptable in time; with no log backups and full backups only every few weeks, there's no real bound on how much data could be lost
It's the maximum allowed downtime during a restore, which is unrelated to backups
It's a SQL Server configuration setting found in sys.databases
It's the amount of disk space reserved for backup files
questions.explain: RPO measures acceptable data loss, not downtime (that's RTO). With log backups never running and full backups only sporadic and manual, MERSQL01 could lose weeks of data in a failure — an undefined, unacceptable RPO.
